Neural Horizons AI | Friday AI Insights

AI Is Moving Beyond the Screen. It's Starting to Shape the Real World.

This week, AI moved into new territory. From designing physical hardware and powering large-scale infrastructure to open-weight models, agentic coding and robotics, the developments point to a bigger shift in how intelligence will be built into business and everyday operations.

6 NOVEMBER 2026 • WEEKLY AI BRIEFING • UAE | GLOBAL

Welcome to this week's Friday AI Insights.

The AI conversation is expanding. We are moving beyond chatbots, copilots and individual productivity tools towards systems that can help design products, coordinate complex workflows, write and execute code, and interact with the physical world.

At the same time, the infrastructure required to support this progress is becoming a major business story in its own right. Compute capacity, energy, data foundations and model choice are increasingly strategic considerations.

The question for business leaders is no longer simply what AI can do. It is where these capabilities can make a meaningful difference — and what needs to be in place to use them responsibly and profitably.

01 | AI enters the physical world

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helps design a device. From concept to prototype in under a week.

One of the most interesting developments this week came from OpenAI, which described how GPT-6 Astra helped two team members design a hardware device for interacting with Codex.

The project went well beyond generating a concept or sketch. OpenAI used Astra to define functional requirements and work through several parts of the design process, including the enclosure, internal structures, electrical components, printed circuit board layout, user interface, firmware and software integrations.

Two team members completed the design work in under a week alongside their other responsibilities. A contract manufacturer then produced a small batch of prototypes in under a month.

The important detail is that this was not a fully autonomous manufacturing process. OpenAI says the device still required several rounds of human review and iteration before it was ready for manufacturing. Astra did not consistently account for production constraints, tolerances and assembly details.

Why this matters: AI is beginning to contribute across disciplines that traditionally require separate design, engineering and software workflows. The opportunity is not simply faster content or code generation. It is the ability to accelerate complex product development.

For businesses, this raises interesting questions about product development cycles, prototyping costs, engineering capacity and how teams can use AI to move from an idea to a testable solution more quickly.

Read OpenAI's engineering announcement →

OpenAI's account describes an internal prototype project. It should not be interpreted as evidence that AI can independently take a product through manufacturing without engineering oversight.

02 | The UAE AI landscape

ADNOC, OpenAI and G42: AI moves into the heart of the energy business.

Abu Dhabi is continuing to position itself at the centre of enterprise AI adoption. ADNOC's multi-year partnership with OpenAI and G42 is a significant example of AI being applied across a complex industrial value chain.

Announced at ADIPEC on 2 November, the partnership will use OpenAI technology and G42's UAE-based computing infrastructure to coordinate AI agents across business operations.

The initial focus includes field master planning and connecting commercial and operational decisions across production, processing, refining, logistics, sales and trading.

The ambition is significant: rather than optimising individual activities in isolation, AI agents will help evaluate the wider impact of decisions across the business.

The bigger point: the next stage of enterprise AI is not simply about making individual teams faster. It is about connecting intelligence so that decisions in one part of a business can inform decisions everywhere else.

ADNOC also confirmed that more than 40,000 employees have access to ChatGPT Enterprise, with adoption exceeding 97%. This is a powerful signal of the scale at which AI is becoming embedded in major organisations.

03 | Enterprise AI adoption

Multi-agent AI is gaining momentum. But enterprise-wide execution is still rare.

New research from Capgemini highlights the growing move towards multi-agent AI across financial services.

Its World Cloud Report for Financial Services 2027, published on 5 November, found that 59% of financial institutions surveyed are piloting or deploying multi-agent AI systems.

Yet only 10% have achieved enterprise-wide orchestration — the level of coordination needed to run agents across the organisation.

The report also points to technology debt, cloud foundations, governance and security as important barriers to scaling.

From AI pilots to orchestration

The next challenge is coordinating agents, data, systems and decisions across the enterprise.

59% Of financial institutions are piloting or deploying multi-agent AI.
10% Have achieved enterprise-wide agent orchestration.
90% Are using or planning intelligent model routing.

Perhaps the most important finding is that adoption does not automatically translate into returns. Capgemini reports that roughly half of financial services firms cannot consistently demonstrate a return on their agentic AI initiatives.

Our perspective: the challenge is no longer simply getting access to AI. It is establishing the data, governance, architecture and accountability required to make AI work across the business — and proving what it delivers.

04 | AI infrastructure and open models

The AI race is expanding. Infrastructure, model choice and execution all matter.

This week's developments reveal another side of the AI transition: the models are evolving, but so are the economics and infrastructure required to build and deploy them.

A $28 billion AI infrastructure deal in Texas

Riot Platforms has signed a 15-year powered-land lease with a frontier AI lab for its Corsicana campus in Texas. The agreement covers 910 MW of critical IT capacity and is expected to generate approximately $28 billion in total contract revenue over the initial lease term.

The project is expected to be delivered in phases, beginning in 2027. The tenant will develop and operate the data-centre compute deployment, while Riot provides the land, powered infrastructure and related facilities.

The scale is significant. AI infrastructure is no longer just a technology procurement issue. It is becoming a major question of energy availability, capital investment, land, construction and long-term capacity planning.

The business implication: the cost and availability of compute will influence which AI capabilities organisations can access, where they deploy them and how they structure their long-term technology strategies.

Read Riot Platforms' announcement →

The approximately $28 billion figure is the projected total contract value over the initial 15-year term, not an upfront investment. The agreement also includes extension options.

Kimi K3.1 Pro: another development in open-weight AI

Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro is part of the growing movement towards powerful models whose weights can be made available for external deployment and adaptation.

The model is described as having 2.8 trillion total parameters, with 104 billion active per token, and a context window of approximately one million tokens.

For enterprise leaders, the significance is the expanding range of model choices. Open-weight models may offer greater control over deployment, customisation and infrastructure decisions, depending on licensing and technical requirements.

More model choice. More responsibility.

Open weights do not automatically mean low-cost deployment. Organisations still need to consider hardware, hosting, security, licensing, maintenance and operational support.

Read the Kimi K3.1 Pro update →

Ripple-65B: a smaller model makes a big coding claim

Ricursive Intelligence has released Ripple-65B Preview, a 65-billion-parameter open-weight model designed with a particular focus on reasoning and agentic coding.

Ricursive reports a score of 80.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, claiming US open-weight state-of-the-art performance against the models included in its comparison. The company also says the model supports up to a one-million-token context window.

The interesting point is not simply the benchmark score. Ripple is a reminder that model size alone does not determine usefulness. Architecture, training, inference efficiency, hardware requirements and the task being performed all matter.

Our perspective: enterprises should not select a model based on headline benchmarks alone. The right model is the one that performs reliably on the organisation's actual workflows, within its cost, security and governance requirements.

Terminal-Bench results cited here are reported by Ricursive. Benchmark performance can vary with evaluation harness, configuration and testing conditions.

05 | Robotics and physical AI

Meet Stringman. An $800 open-source room-scale robot.

Not every important development in AI is happening inside a data centre or on a computer screen. Robotics continues to explore how intelligent systems can interact with the physical environment.

Stringman is an open-source room-scale gripper robot built around a cable-driven design. Its reported cost is approximately $800, with the project sharing hardware and software resources for others to explore and develop.

The design is interesting because it takes a different approach to physical movement and manipulation. Rather than relying on a conventional robotic arm, its cable-driven arrangement offers a way to move a gripper through a larger working space.

It is an experimental project, not a ready-made industrial automation solution. But it is another example of how accessible hardware, open designs and AI research are contributing to the wider robotics ecosystem.

Why keep an eye on this: as robotics becomes more accessible, businesses will have more opportunities to explore automation in environments where traditional industrial robotics may be too expensive or inflexible.

06 | Data and infrastructure

AI agents need more than data. They need to understand the business behind it.

Oracle's announcement of new capabilities for its Autonomous AI Lakehouse highlights the importance of business context in enterprise AI.

The updates include a business semantic layer designed to give AI agents and users better access to business context, alongside expanded support for data across enterprise environments.

Giving an agent access to information does not mean it understands what that information represents, how the organisation defines it, or which rules govern its use.

Different departments may use the same business term but define it differently. An AI agent working across those departments needs consistent definitions and reliable context before it can make useful decisions.

The takeaway: enterprise AI depends on business context. Data quality, shared definitions, permissions and governance are essential to making intelligent systems useful.

07 | From insight to implementation
Neural Horizons AI | FMCG case study

Before building AI agents, we asked a different question: Which ones were actually ready?

In a regional FMCG and manufacturing engagement, our readiness evaluation examined 541,194 invoice lines and assessed eight proposed AI agents against four practical readiness gates.

The diagnostic uncovered significant value at stake across the operation. More than 20,000 orders had been cancelled after the delivery plan was already built, representing approximately AED 2.82 million in the year examined.

A separate network inefficiency represented approximately AED 5.49 million in annual value at stake. Peak van-sales returns were also running at 28.8%.

541,194 Invoice lines examined.
8 Candidate AI agents assessed.
2 Agents cleared all readiness gates for immediate build.
AED 5.49M Annual value at stake from identified network inefficiency.

Why only two agents passed

Every proposed agent was assessed against four gates:

  • Data: Does the required data exist, and is it reliable?
  • Definition: Is there an agreed definition of what the agent is deciding?
  • Governance: Is there a named human owner and approval process?
  • Freedom to act: Is the agent blocked by another system or migration dependency?

Two agents cleared all four gates: one focused on network and cost-to-serve optimisation, and another on cancelled-order validation. The remaining six required further data, governance or system readiness work before development.

The lesson: a good AI idea is not necessarily a ready AI use case. Establishing readiness before development protects investment, focuses resources and gives leadership a clearer path to measurable outcomes.

Phase 2 is progressing through a 100-day implementation plan. The two approved agents are moving into build, while readiness gaps affecting the remaining use cases are addressed in parallel.

The figures represent findings and value identified during the diagnostic. They are not presented as realised savings. Implementation is in progress.

09 | The bigger picture

The next AI advantage will come from how businesses connect the dots.

This week's developments point in the same direction: AI is becoming more capable, more connected and increasingly embedded in the physical and commercial world.

OpenAI's hardware experiment shows how AI can contribute across product design and engineering. Riot's infrastructure agreement demonstrates the scale of investment required to support frontier AI. New open-weight models are expanding the choices available to developers and enterprises, while agentic coding and robotics are pushing the boundaries of what intelligent systems can do.

At the enterprise level, ADNOC is connecting intelligence across an entire energy value chain. Financial institutions are moving towards multi-agent systems, while discovering that orchestration, governance and measurable returns remain difficult to achieve. Technology providers are strengthening the data foundations that agents need to understand business context.

The opportunity is substantial, but so is the responsibility to implement AI with purpose.

Businesses do not need more disconnected pilots, dashboards or tools that solve one problem while creating another. They need a clear understanding of where value is being lost, which processes are ready to change, and how intelligence can connect the organisation.

Our view at Neural Horizons AI: Start with the business problem. Understand the data. Establish readiness. Build around measurable outcomes. AI is simply one tool — the value comes from what it enables the business to do.
